hints: Remember how electronegativity changes across a Period, it increases from left to right as nuclear charge increases.
L has the highest value from Na to Cl so L must be chlorine, while M has the lowest value so M must be sodium.
Now think about what $\text{Cl}_2$ looks like on its own, and what happens when very different elements like Na and Cl join together.
walkthrough:
**Identify L and M from electronegativity**

Electronegativity increases across Period 3 from left to right. The least electronegative is on the left, the most is on the right.

So for Na to Cl: $M = \text{Na}$ (lowest), $L = \text{Cl}$ (highest).

**Check statements 1 and 2**

Statement 1: Chlorine exists as $\text{Cl}_2$ molecules held by a shared pair of electrons. That is a covalent bond, so statement 1 is true.

Statement 2: Atomic number increases across the period. $\text{Cl}$ is atomic number 17, $\text{Na}$ is 11, so L > M and statement 2 is true.

**Check statement 3 about the compound**

A compound of Na and Cl is $\text{NaCl}$. The electronegativity difference is very large.

$$\text{Na (low EN) + Cl (high EN)} \rightarrow \text{Na}^+ + \text{Cl}^-$$
This electron transfer gives ionic bonding, so statement 3 is true. All three are correct.

options.A: All three statements are true. L is Cl which forms covalent $\text{Cl}_2$, L (17) has higher atomic number than M, Na (11), and $\text{NaCl}$ is a classic ionic compound.
options.B: This misses statement 3. Students may forget that a very large electronegativity difference between Na and Cl leads to electron transfer and ionic bonding in $\text{NaCl}$.
options.C: This misses statement 2. Students may mix up the direction of the electronegativity trend and think highest electronegativity means lowest atomic number, but across a period both increase to the right.
options.D: This misses statement 1. Students may think chlorine as an element has no bonds or has ionic bonds, but $\text{Cl}_2$ is a simple covalent molecule.
